summary.title: A Note on Essential Complexity
summary.one_liner: Essential complexity may be reducible by redefining the problem and getting the world to conform to software, not only by changing the software itself.
takeaways: Essential complexity is defined from the user's point of view: if the team could avoid a complexity and users would still accept the system, it is accidental.
Brooks's 'No Silver Bullet' and Moseley and Marks's 'Out of the Tar Pit' treat essential complexity as irreducible by software redesign alone.
The author argues essential complexity can be reduced by redefining the problem, since software can shape user behavior and organizations.
For legacy systems with no clear specification, turning systems off to see who complains is a way to gain information and remove unneeded complexity.
The author cautions that engineers should not take complexity reduction to extremes, and should consider economic interests and their impact on people.
summary.summary: The essay starts by listing the many goals that can be called the job of a software engineer, then picks managing complexity as the main duty. It draws on Ousterhout, Brooks's No Silver Bullet, and Moseley and Marks's Out of the Tar Pit to define essential versus accidental complexity from the user's perspective. The author then challenges the idea that essential complexity is irreducible, arguing that software can reshape user expectations and organizations, and that questioning requirements and running shutdown experiments on legacy systems can reduce complexity. It closes by warning that taking this to the extreme ignores economic realities and the human impact of engineering work.
